Lemoine Gen

GeometryTrianglesConstructions
Game: This is a drawing to explore, not a game to win: watch two paths keep landing on the sides of a triangle.
How to play: Drag A, B, C or M with a mouse or finger, or focus one and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show the paths and their centre, and press Step or Animate to draw more steps.
Look for the math

The live cut-the-knot page gives only the title “Generalization of Lemoine iterations” and the Java applet; a 2020 archive has the same applet and no further text. The exact claim ported here is therefore the one the code carries: two walks from a free point M keep landing on the side lines, and the marked centre is computed from M's position in a fixed way. The logic test checks both on 600 seeded triangles and compares every construction with a second transcription of the bytecode.

Two walks around the triangle

Start from any point P. The red step for side BC draws the line through P parallel to AM and meets it with BC. The next red step uses BM and CA, then CM and AB, and repeats. The blue step instead drops a perpendicular from P to a side and then uses the same side as the red step: the order is BC, CA, AB for red and BC, AB, CA for blue, exactly as the applet's index switch does. Each step is an affine map of the plane, so after three steps each walk induces a map of one side line to itself. The test follows both walks for many steps and confirms that each one settles into a repeating three-point cycle, with one point on each side line.

The centre the applet marks

Write M in barycentric coordinates M = (x : y : z) with respect to ABC. The applet's ComputeCenter forms (1/x : 1/y : 1/z) and then returns (1/y + 1/z : 1/z + 1/x : 1/x + 1/y). In other words it first takes the isotomic conjugate of M and then the complement of that point: halve the sum of its three coordinates to place the centroid-based midpoint. The logic test compares this with a separate transcription of the bytecode on 600 triangles. Drag M: the green dot follows this formula, not the last point of either walk.

Back to ordinary Lemoine iterations

When M is the symmedian point K = (a² : b² : c²), the red walk is the classical Lemoine construction with lines parallel to the symmedians. The marked centre becomes (1/b² + 1/c² : 1/c² + 1/a² : 1/a² + 1/b²). The test checks this identity and checks that the two walks still settle on the sides, so the generalisation agrees with the familiar case at its special point. The page itself states no minimum count or inequality, so none is asserted here.

Try ticking Connections and then dragging M across a side: watch how the centre moves as M leaves the triangle.
